visual_source_files.evidence: Public 1328×674 PNG contains the same two BRIGHT/BEIR bar-panel layout and opacity/legend grammar as PDF Fig. 3, but its BRIGHT values and caption/references differ from the PDF; it is a related rendered asset, not an exact numeric source.
Public 1316×638 PNG reproduces the Table 1 CoIR result grid and values/gray/bold conventions, with a slightly different caption year and rendering; it is the closest rendered table source.
Repository README title, abstract, paper link, result images, resources, and training/evaluation instructions directly identify the Revela paper and embed the two visual assets.

source_acquisition.search_note: PDF fact source: corpus/pdfs/iclr-2026-6f113e6f8081.pdf, 24 pages, fully rendered at 200 dpi to /tmp/visual-audit-iclr-2026-6f113e6f8081-20260828/pages/page-01.png … page-24.png; references occupy pp.11–14 and were read, with no Figure/Table there. The PDF inventory contains 7 Figures and 19 Tables, all recorded. The local corpus/visual_sources/iclr-2026-6f113e6f8081 directory is absent. The title footnote on p.1, OpenReview URL, repository metadata, and README title establish TRUMANCFY/Revela as the direct public repository. Its recursive tree has 37 entries and only two rendered result assets (assets/bright_beir.png and assets/coir.png) plus implementation code; no plot*, table*, .ipynb, .tex, .tikz, .pgf, .svg, or editable figure source was found. bright_beir.png matches the Fig. 3 structure but has different BRIGHT values than the PDF; coir.png matches the Table 1 grid closely but carries a different citation year. Therefore this is a partial rendered visual source, not an exact all-object generator. PDF pages also show colored hyperlink annotation rectangles around citations/URLs; these are PDF navigation artifacts, not data encodings.

paper_style.palette_strategy: The paper uses restrained categorical colors for benchmark/model families and topic/semantic examples, with opacity and bold as secondary cues. Figure 1/2 use colored blocks and attention states; Figures 3–5 use Matplotlib-like bars; Figures 6–7 use semantic chunk colors. Hyperlink annotation rectangles in red/green/cyan appear throughout the rendered PDF but are navigation artifacts rather than visual encodings.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: The PDF is predominantly vector: Figures 2–7, chart bars, table rules, captions, and prompt/text blocks render as vector text/rules; Figure 1 mixes vector flow elements with embedded raster text/icon snippets. The public repository supplies only raster PNG counterparts for the main CoIR table and BRIGHT/BEIR bar chart, and no editable source for the remaining objects.
paper_style.style_consistency: ICLR serif/Computer Modern text, compact booktabs tables, direct value labels, and repeated nDCG@10 (%) notation form a coherent result language. The dense page-width main table and appendix matrices prioritize completeness over scanability; chart fonts are visibly sans-serif while captions/tables remain serif.

figures.label: Fig. 1

caption.text: Figure 1: The framework of Revela. The retriever’s in-batch similarity scores are used as in-batch attention weights inside transformer blocks. The retriever is trained by optimizing the language modeling objective, i.e., NTP. The related patterns in red and purple sequences are highlighted in bold and underline. An example of training dynamics is illustrated at App. A.

color.semantic_mapping: Blue/red/yellow/purple chunk fills identify example text groups; colored arrows and the vertical retriever indicate similarity flow and the red/purple highlighted patterns.

encodings.line: arrows from chunks → retriever/similarity → in-batch attention → NTP/backprop
encodings.facet: batch, similarity, transformer, and output stages
encodings.text: chunk text, PPL/NTP, similarity scores, self/in-batch attention labels

figures.data_and_statistics: A wide framework schematic shows colored text chunks entering a dense retriever, similarity scores becoming in-batch attention weights, transformer self-attention/in-batch-attention blocks, and next-token prediction with backpropagation. Related red and purple text patterns are also bold/underlined. It has no numeric axes or uncertainty display.
figures.evidence_relation: Introduction claim about learning document dependencies from NTP → Fig. 1 fixes the batch-to-retriever-to-attention interface → §3 and Eq. (1)–(7) formalize it → Table 1/Fig. 3 evaluate retrieval results; App. A Fig. 6 supplies training dynamics. Page 2 contains several embedded raster snippets, so the figure is mixed rather than pure vector.
design_strengths: The left-to-right causal/data-flow order is legible and ties the retriever to LM loss.
The same color groups recur in chunks, similarity links, and outputs, making relatedness concrete.
The caption names NTP and the Appendix A continuation.
design_weaknesses: Many small token strings and repeated transformer blocks are hard to read at normal two-column scale.
Color, bold, and underline carry overlapping semantics without a compact legend.
The figure shows a conceptual path but not tensor dimensions, batch masking, or the exact normalization.
figures.reusable_pattern: For a new training signal, place raw examples, the learned similarity/weighting interface, the modified block, and the optimization target on one directed canvas.

figures.label: Fig. 2

caption.text: Figure 2: Revela’s architecture. With an attention map, the embeddings of in-batch attention {h_i^l}_{i=1}^B can attend to the self-attention {e_i^l}_{i=1}^B.

color.semantic_mapping: Green and pink legend swatches distinguish self-attention and in-batch attention; blue/purple/yellow boxes identify embeddings, retriever/similarity, and transformer stages.

encodings.line: arrows through retriever, embeddings, attention, FFN, softmax
encodings.text: Similarity Matrix, Retriever, In-Batch Attention, Self-Attention, Output Probabilities

figures.data_and_statistics: The architecture diagram pairs a vertical module pipeline with an attention-map inset. Document embeddings feed a retriever/similarity matrix; in-batch attention and self-attention are stacked through layer norm/feed-forward blocks, ending in linear/softmax output probabilities. The inset uses green/pink cells and dashed/solid regions to show which embeddings attend to which states; no numeric scale or uncertainty is present.
figures.evidence_relation: §3.1–§3.4 method equations → Fig. 2 shows where in-batch attention is inserted and how the mask is organized → Eq. (5)–(7) define cross-document aggregation → Fig. 1 provides the high-level story and Table 2 isolates the resulting retriever behavior.
design_strengths: The attention-map inset closes the gap between a conceptual architecture and its mask operation.
The color key is local and the pipeline arrows make optional similarity computation visible.
Vector rules/text remain crisp in the PDF.
design_weaknesses: The figure is dense for a single column and the smallest symbols are difficult to decode.
The same two hues must be distinguished against pale block fills; grayscale loses the attention distinction.
The diagram omits the exact document/token tensor shapes and how duplicated streams are concatenated.
figures.reusable_pattern: Show the architectural insertion point beside a small mask/attention map, with the dataflow and semantic color key sharing the same coordinate system.

figures.label: Fig. 3

caption.text: Figure 3: Performance on BRIGHT (left) and BEIR (right) (nDCG@10, %). Results for Revela are shown in opaque bars, while all other models are represented by transparent bars. On BRIGHT, Revela3B surpasses E5-Mistral, a supervised retriever with more parameters, and properties APIs. On BEIR, Revela achieves similar performance with E5-PT with much less data and compute. Please refer to Tab. 7 and Tab. 8 in App. B.6 for the per-task results.

color.semantic_mapping: Bar opacity identifies Revela (opaque) versus other models (transparent); hue groups unsupervised, supervised, sparse, commercial API, and GPU-hour categories in the two panels.

encodings.text: numeric value labels above bars, dataset titles, legend swatches

figures.data_and_statistics: Two side-by-side bar panels report mean nDCG@10 (%) for 12 BRIGHT subtasks and 13 BEIR tasks. Bars have numeric value labels, truncated/rotated model labels, and separate legends; y-axes are linear but ranges differ (BRIGHT roughly 0–25, BEIR roughly 0–50). No error bars or distribution marks are shown.
figures.evidence_relation: The main Table 1 CoIR comparison → Fig. 3 broadens the headline across reasoning-intensive BRIGHT and general BEIR and foregrounds data/compute context → App. B.6 Tables 7–8 provide per-task values; Fig. 4/5 and Tables 11–18 test scaling and domain robustness.
design_strengths: Opaque/transparent bars make the proposed model visually prominent without adding another panel.
Direct value labels avoid reading small y ticks for the headline means.
The two benchmark panels share a familiar bar grammar and fit the page width.
design_weaknesses: Different y-axis maxima make visual bar heights incomparable across BRIGHT and BEIR.
Opacity and multiple hue categories are not robust in grayscale; API/compute semantics require the legend.
Mean-only bars hide per-task heterogeneity, which is substantial in Tables 7–8.
The current GitHub bright_beir.png is structurally similar but has different BRIGHT values, so it is not an exact numeric source for this PDF figure.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use paired benchmark panels with direct value labels and a baseline/promoted-model opacity convention, but retain matched y limits or a visible scale warning when comparing panels.

figures.label: Fig. 4

caption.text: Figure 4: Performance comparison on CoIR and BEIR with different batch sizes. For both benchmarks, Revela performance generally scales with batch size.

color.semantic_mapping: Blue/orange/green bars encode batch sizes 4/8/16 in both CoIR and BEIR panels.

figures.data_and_statistics: Two bar panels compare mean nDCG@10 (%) for three retriever backbones at batch sizes 4, 8, and 16. CoIR and BEIR use separate linear y ranges (approximately 40–60 and 20–45); there are no error bars or per-task marks.
figures.evidence_relation: The analysis question about in-batch negatives → Fig. 4 tests the batch-size factor → Tables 11–12 supply all CoIR/BEIR task rows → the main Fig. 3 and Table 1 provide the default batch-size context.
design_strengths: The repeated three-color batch key makes the monotonic trend easy to scan.
The same retriever x-axis categories are used in both benchmark panels.
The caption states the directional finding directly.
design_weaknesses: Separate y-axis ranges can exaggerate or mute cross-benchmark differences.
Color alone carries batch identity and the legend is repeated rather than encoded in bar patterns.
Mean bars do not show whether larger batches help every task.
figures.reusable_pattern: Keep a scaling ablation to two matched panels with the factor as color and the backbone as x; attach a complete per-task table when the mean trend is the claim.

figures.label: Fig. 5

caption.text: Figure 5: Performance comparison on CoIR and BEIR using various combinations of retrievers and LMs. For code retrieval tasks, larger LMs can yield greater gains in retriever performance.

color.semantic_mapping: Blue/orange/green bars encode LM sizes SmolLM2-135M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, and LLaMA-3.2-1B in both panels.

figures.data_and_statistics: Two bar panels compare mean nDCG@10 (%) for three retriever sizes crossed with three LM sizes. The CoIR panel supports the caption’s larger-LM trend; the BEIR panel shows a weaker/non-monotonic pattern. Linear y-axes and no uncertainty bars are used.
figures.evidence_relation: The scaling question in §5 → Fig. 5 isolates LM size while Fig. 4 isolates batch size → Tables 13–14 provide per-task LM-size rows → Tables 15–18 test whether the pattern survives mixed or out-of-domain training.
design_strengths: A consistent x-axis and color key make the retriever/LM cross-factor visible.
The paired CoIR/BEIR panels show domain dependence rather than claiming one universal scaling curve.
The caption supplies the code-retrieval interpretation.
design_weaknesses: The three-by-three bars are dense and rely on a small color legend.
Different y limits again hinder direct visual comparison of absolute performance.
No uncertainty or statistical test distinguishes a real LM-size effect from task-average variation.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use factorial grouped bars for a small scaling design, then move to per-task or interaction tables when the trend can change by domain.

figures.label: Fig. 6

caption.text: Figure 6: Example of training dynamics of Revela. The related patterns in red and purple sequences are highlighted in bold, underline, and italic.

color.semantic_mapping: Blue/yellow and red/purple identify semantically related chunk pairs; colored borders and text emphasis (bold/underline/italic) redundantly mark the patterns, while gray cells are low similarity.

encodings.text: chunk text, matrix values, Loss labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Three checkpoint columns combine highlighted Wikipedia-like chunk text, a 4×4 similarity matrix, and a scalar LM loss: Init/Loss 4.86, Step 100/Loss 4.59, Step 200/Loss 4.52. Matrix cells contain numeric probabilities; no axes, uncertainty, or error bars are present.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix A explains the training-dynamics intuition introduced by Fig. 1 → Fig. 6 shows related chunk pairs becoming concentrated as loss falls → the main method equations define the similarity/NTP coupling. It is a qualitative mechanism check, not an inferential training curve.
design_strengths: The three checkpoints establish a temporal reading order without requiring a separate legend.
Numeric cells and text highlighting connect semantic relevance to the learned similarity matrix.
The loss label supplies a compact quantitative anchor for the qualitative example.
design_weaknesses: The matrices are tiny and values are hard to compare across checkpoints.
Blue/yellow/red/purple encodings and text styles are visually busy and not fully grayscale safe.
Only one example and three snapshots are shown; no aggregate convergence distribution is provided.
figures.reusable_pattern: Show an illustrative training trajectory as aligned example text, a small relation matrix, and one scalar objective at each checkpoint, while explicitly labeling it as qualitative.

figures.label: Fig. 7

caption.text: Figure 7: Example of one batch containing chunks split from Wikipedia: This batch contains chunks from two topics: Alcohol (blue) and Achill Island topic (green).

color.semantic_mapping: Blue and green rounded chunk boxes identify Alcohol and Achill Island topics; white background separates the two topic blocks.

encodings.facet: two topic sections within one 16-chunk batch
encodings.text: chunk numbers, topic headings, text snippets

figures.data_and_statistics: A qualitative batch display lists 16 sentence chunks from Alcohol and Achill Island, with topic-colored rounded boxes. The order is illustrative and the appendix text says chunks are randomly shuffled during training; there are no axes, quantitative marks, or uncertainty encodings.
figures.evidence_relation: §4.1 describes chunking and random batch construction → Fig. 7 makes a heterogeneous 16-chunk batch concrete → Fig. 1’s batch-to-attention mechanism and Tables 3–4’s benchmark task inventories provide context.
design_strengths: The two topic colors make cross-document composition immediately visible.
Numbering preserves batch order while the text snippets show realistic chunk granularity.
The caption explains both topic semantics and the source of the chunks.
design_weaknesses: The screenshot-like text is dense and requires close zoom.
Topic color is the only semantic separator beyond headings and is weak in grayscale.
One hand-selected batch cannot establish typical topic mixing or hard-negative frequency.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a color-coded batch example to expose the granularity and heterogeneity that a cross-document training mechanism consumes; follow it with the formal batching rule.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1: Performance on CoIR (nDCG@10, %). Gray indicates supervised models. Bold marks the highest score among non-API models in each row. Columns marked † used code-related pairs during pre-training. The results of APIs are collected from Li et al. (2025). Without query-document pairs, Revela3B surpasses larger supervised models and proprietary APIs, averaged across 10 tasks.

tables.uncertainty: nDCG@10 (%) is reported per CoIR task and as an unweighted Mean row; all values are point estimates with no variance, interval, significance test, or per-task failure count.
tables.data_and_statistics: Dataset plus 13 model columns: sparse BM25, supervised UniX/BGE/E5-Mistral, self/weakly supervised E5-PT/REPLUG, Revela at multiple sizes, and two APIs. Two header levels give model size beneath model names. Gray columns mark supervised models; bold is the best non-API value in each row; dagger columns used code-related pretraining pairs.
tables.evidence_relation: The self-supervised retriever claim → Table 1 is the CoIR headline comparison → Fig. 3 extends the same mean nDCG@10 framing to BRIGHT/BEIR → Tables 9/10 provide controlled per-task Revela-vs-Contriever checks.
design_strengths: A wide model header keeps scale and family visible above every task row.
Gray/bold conventions make the proposed-vs-supervised comparison fast to scan.
The Mean row directly supports the headline 10-task claim.
design_weaknesses: Thirteen numeric columns force very small type and long method labels.
Gray cell fill is not robust in grayscale or on low-contrast displays.
The mean can conceal task-level reversals visible in Appendix B.6; no uncertainty accompanies close values.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use one wide leaderboard for the headline, but preserve model size and training provenance in a second header row and pair aggregate means with per-task appendix tables.

tables.label: Table 2

caption.text: Table 2: Revela vs. Contriever Performance.

tables.uncertainty: BEIR, CoIR, and AVG are nDCG@10 (%) point estimates for matched LLaMA-3.2-1B Revela and Contriever runs; no uncertainty or task-level breakdown is shown here.
tables.data_and_statistics: Four rows compare Revela-wiki, Contriever-wiki, Revela-code, and Contriever-code under three metric columns (BEIR, CoIR, AVG) plus Model. Horizontal rules separate Wikipedia/code training rows; bold marks higher cells in the PDF.
tables.evidence_relation: The analysis section’s matched-backbone question → Table 2 isolates Revela’s in-batch/NTP algorithm from backbone and data differences → Tables 9–10 unpack task-level reversals; Fig. 4–5 test other factors.
design_strengths: The compact four-row structure makes the controlled comparison easy to read beside the analysis text.
BEIR and CoIR are placed beside AVG, exposing cross-domain trade-offs.
Wiki/code row grouping maps directly to the training-data factor.
design_weaknesses: The terse caption does not define nDCG@10, AVG, training corpus, or the bolding rule.
Averaging two benchmarks hides task-level gains and losses.
The double-column placement leaves little room for explanatory headers or resource columns.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a compact matched-backbone table for a causal ablation, but define the estimand and keep the full task rows in an adjacent appendix table.

tables.label: Table 3

caption.text: Table 3: CoIR Benchmark Tasks. The superscripts present the type of the tasks. The abbreviation of the tasks is noted in the parentheses, presented in Table 1.

tables.uncertainty: Static benchmark metadata: task names and prose descriptions; no numeric evaluation statistic or uncertainty field.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two columns (Sub-Tasks (Abbr.), Descriptions) and ten CoIR task rows. Superscripts encode four task classes (Text-to-Code, Code-to-Code, Code-to-Text, Hybrid); there are no explicit row separators between classes.
tables.evidence_relation: §4.1 introduces CoIR → Table 3 defines the abbreviations used in Table 1 and Appendix Tables 9, 11, 14, 15, and 17 → it is a dataset/reproduction key rather than a result table.
design_strengths: Descriptions are sufficiently concrete to identify the retrieval operation.
Superscripts compactly retain the four class taxonomy.
The table is narrow and readable compared with result matrices.
design_weaknesses: Class boundaries are not visually grouped beyond superscripts.
The caption points to Table 1 for abbreviations rather than repeating the evaluation protocol.
No dataset sizes or train/test split counts are included.
tables.reusable_pattern: Keep benchmark taxonomies in a two-column glossary with the exact abbreviations used by result tables, and add explicit class grouping when taxonomy matters.

tables.label: Table 4

caption.text: Table 4: BRIGHT Benchmark Tasks. Abbreviations and descriptions.

tables.uncertainty: Static benchmark metadata: BRIGHT subtask abbreviations and descriptions; no numeric statistic or uncertainty field.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two columns (Abbrev., Description) and twelve BRIGHT subtask rows. The list spans StackExchange biology/economics/psychology/robotics/sustainability, StackOverflow, coding, and theorem/math tasks with no additional numeric columns.
tables.evidence_relation: §4.1 introduces BRIGHT → Table 4 defines the abbreviations behind Figure 3 and Table 8’s per-task rows → it establishes the denominator of the BRIGHT mean.
design_strengths: The descriptions explain the domain and retrieval context in one line each.
The list is compact and directly maps to the result-table task names.
No unnecessary numeric columns dilute the glossary purpose.
design_weaknesses: The diverse domains are not grouped visually, so the taxonomy must be read row by row.
The caption does not state the 12-task denominator used for reported means.
No source/license column accompanies the benchmark names.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a short benchmark glossary to make every result-table abbreviation auditable; state the task count and source next to the glossary.

tables.label: Table 5

caption.text: Table 5: Baseline retrievers, LMs (Revela’s backbone), CodeRAG-Bench datasets, and evaluation benchmarks with their HuggingFace URLs and licenses.

tables.uncertainty: Resource metadata only: names, URLs, and licenses; no performance values, counts, uncertainty, or cost estimates.
tables.data_and_statistics: Three columns (Name, URL, License) and four row groups: baseline retrievers, LM backbones, CodeRAG-Bench datasets, and BEIR/CoIR benchmarks. Long HuggingFace identifiers are rendered as cyan hyperlink boxes in the PDF.
tables.evidence_relation: §4.1’s model/baseline definitions → Table 5 exposes the checkpoints and licenses needed to reproduce Tables 1–2 and Figures 3–5 → Table 6 separately lists API embedding references.
design_strengths: Grouping by resource role makes the reproduction inventory navigable.
The URL and license columns are actionable rather than merely naming models.
The table includes both benchmark and training-corpus resources.
design_weaknesses: URLs are long and the visible hyperlink annotation boxes add visual noise.
“Not specified” licenses leave a reproducibility/legal gap.
No revision/commit/date column fixes the resource versions.
tables.reusable_pattern: Publish a resource table with role groups, exact URLs, licenses, and version/revision columns; keep it separate from numeric results.

tables.label: Table 6

caption.text: Table 6: Embedding models and their reference URLs.

tables.uncertainty: Resource metadata only: embedding-model names and reference URLs; no scores, uncertainty, or API cost field.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two columns (Name, URL) and five API/embedding model rows: OpenAI-Ada-002, Voyage-code-2, text-embedding-3-large, voyage-large-2-instruct, and Cohere-embed-english-v3.0.
tables.evidence_relation: Figure 3’s proprietary/API bars → Table 6 supplies the external reference URLs → Table 1 and Figure 3 identify the API comparisons, while Table 5 covers open checkpoints.
design_strengths: The short table makes each API reference easy to locate.
Separating APIs from checkpoints clarifies access modality.
The two-column layout avoids crowding the main result table.
design_weaknesses: No API version/date, pricing, query limits, or retrieval configuration is recorded.
Long URLs still require small type and hyperlink boxes.
The caption does not identify which benchmark each model supports.
tables.reusable_pattern: Track API resources in a dedicated two-column table but include version, date, endpoint, and benchmark-use columns for durable reproduction.

tables.label: Table 7

caption.text: Table 7: Performance of unsupervised/self-supervised retriever models on BEIR datasets (nDCG@10, %). Bold marks the best score per dataset among unsupervised methods.

tables.uncertainty: nDCG@10 (%) per 13 BEIR tasks plus Mean; point estimates only, no variance, interval, significance, or per-task failure indicator.
tables.data_and_statistics: Dataset plus twelve model columns (BM25, Contriever, LaPraDor, Revela/E5/REPLUG variants from 0.1B–3B). Two header levels give model size below model family. Bold marks the best unsupervised/self-supervised method per dataset; Mean is a separate final row.
tables.evidence_relation: Figure 3’s BEIR mean → Table 7 supplies the 13 task values and explains why mean parity can coexist with task wins/losses → Table 10 is the matched Contriever control; Tables 12–18 extend scaling/domain slices.
design_strengths: The full task grid prevents the headline mean from hiding domain-specific reversals.
Model-size header keeps scaling comparisons auditable.
Bold is restricted to the stated unsupervised subset.
design_weaknesses: Thirteen numeric columns and long dataset names are very dense.
Comparability across baselines is complicated by different training data and resource classes.
No uncertainty or task-level significance makes close bold differences descriptive only.
tables.reusable_pattern: Make the aggregate headline reproducible with a per-task matrix that preserves model size and the exact method subset used for highlighting.

tables.label: Table 8

caption.text: Table 8: Performance on BRIGHT (nDCG@10, %). Bold marks the best performance. The results of BM25, E5-Mistral and APIs are taken from BRIGHT (Hongjin et al., 2025).

tables.uncertainty: nDCG@10 (%) per 12 BRIGHT tasks plus Mean; point estimates only. BM25, E5-Mistral, and API values are imported from the BRIGHT source; no uncertainty is reported.
tables.data_and_statistics: Dataset plus ten model/API columns with a two-level model-size header. Bold marks the best performance in each task/Mean row; the table mixes sparse, self-supervised, supervised, REPLUG, and commercial API systems.
tables.evidence_relation: Figure 3’s BRIGHT mean → Table 8 supplies the 12 task values and external-source provenance → Table 4 defines task abbreviations and Table 7 supplies the parallel BEIR view.
design_strengths: The table preserves the cross-domain task heterogeneity behind the BRIGHT claim.
Source provenance for imported baseline/API values is stated in the caption.
A common task/Mean structure makes it comparable with Table 7.
design_weaknesses: The mixed baseline provenance complicates a causal comparison.
Eleven logical columns plus long names make the table hard to scan.
No uncertainty or per-task retrieval counts accompany the mean.
tables.reusable_pattern: Pair every benchmark mean chart with a per-task table and state which baselines are imported versus recomputed.

tables.label: Table 9

caption.text: Table 9: Performance on CoIR (nDCG@10, %). Bold marks the best score among the models.

tables.uncertainty: nDCG@10 (%) per 10 CoIR tasks plus Mean for two matched Wikipedia/code Revela-vs-Contriever pairs; point estimates only.
tables.data_and_statistics: Dataset plus four model columns: Revela-wiki1B, Contriever-wiki1B, Revela-code1B, Contriever-code1B. One header level, one task block, bold best score per task, and a Mean row.
tables.evidence_relation: Table 2’s controlled aggregate → Table 9 exposes task-level CoIR wins/reversals under the same LM/data choices → Table 3 defines task abbreviations and Tables 15/17 test mixed/OOD alternatives.
design_strengths: The four-column layout isolates the training-method contrast cleanly.
The task rows reveal that aggregate CoIR gains are not universal.
Bold per-row comparison is easy to interpret.
design_weaknesses: No explicit paired difference column summarizes the control effect.
The narrow table omits resource/compute details already described in prose.
No variance or repeated-run information is provided.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a small per-task controlled table beside an aggregate ablation so algorithmic claims are not supported by means alone.

tables.label: Table 10

caption.text: Table 10: Performance of unsupervised/self-supervised retriever models on BEIR datasets (nDCG@10, %). Bold marks the best score per dataset.

tables.uncertainty: nDCG@10 (%) per 13 BEIR tasks plus Mean for two matched Wikipedia/code Revela-vs-Contriever pairs; point estimates only.
tables.data_and_statistics: Dataset plus four model columns, same header as Table 9, with 13 task rows and Mean. Bold marks the best per task. The table is wider than Table 9 only because dataset names and rows fill the page, not because more model columns are added.
tables.evidence_relation: Table 2’s BEIR aggregate → Table 10 reveals task-level control differences and the contrast between Wikipedia/code training → Table 7 gives the broader baseline comparison.
design_strengths: Matching the Table 9 header enables direct CoIR/BEIR control comparison.
The task rows expose where Contriever remains better despite a close mean.
Simple booktabs structure keeps the causal comparison legible.
design_weaknesses: A wide page is used for a five-column table, leaving large whitespace.
The caption does not restate matched LM, corpus, or training settings.
No uncertainty or effect-difference column is provided.
tables.reusable_pattern: Keep matched-control tables visually identical across benchmarks and reserve the extra width for explicit difference or resource columns when available.

tables.label: Table 11

caption.text: Table 11: Retrieval performance (nDCG@10, %) across the 10 CoIR tasks. We report three encoder sizes (135M, 500M, 1B) and three batch sizes (bs4, bs8, bs16).

tables.uncertainty: nDCG@10 (%) across 10 CoIR tasks plus Mean; three retriever sizes × three batch sizes, point estimates without uncertainty.
tables.data_and_statistics: Dataset plus nine numeric columns grouped under Revela0.1B, Revela0.5B, Revela1B; each group has bs4, bs8, bs16 subcolumns. Bold is used in the Mean row/row-wise best values in the PDF.
tables.evidence_relation: Figure 4’s CoIR batch-size trend → Table 11 provides every task and retriever-size combination → Table 12 is the BEIR counterpart; Fig. 1/2 motivate why batch composition is a method factor.
design_strengths: Two header levels encode the factorial design without adding separate factor columns.
The three batch-size columns repeat within each retriever group, supporting within-size comparison.
Per-task rows reveal non-monotonic exceptions to the mean trend.
design_weaknesses: Ten numeric columns and long task labels force small type.
Bold/highlight rules are difficult to decode for ties or non-monotonic rows.
No compute or memory cost column accompanies the batch-size factor.
tables.reusable_pattern: Represent a two-factor scaling ablation with nested column groups and a matched per-task table; add resource cost when scale is the practical claim.

tables.label: Table 12

caption.text: Table 12: Retrieval performance (nDCG@10, %) across 13 BEIR tasks for three encoder sizes and three batch sizes (bs4, bs8, bs16).

tables.uncertainty: nDCG@10 (%) across 13 BEIR tasks plus Mean; three retriever sizes × three batch sizes, point estimates without uncertainty.
tables.data_and_statistics: Dataset plus nine numeric columns grouped under Revela0.1B, Revela0.5B, Revela1B, each with bs4/bs8/bs16. Two header levels and a single task block make this the BEIR counterpart to Table 11.
tables.evidence_relation: Figure 4’s BEIR batch-size panel → Table 12 tests whether batch scaling transports to general-domain retrieval → Table 11 and Tables 13–14 separate batch and LM-size factors.
design_strengths: The common design with Table 11 makes cross-benchmark scaling comparisons straightforward.
Nested headers make the factor levels explicit.
The Mean row is easy to locate after the 13 task rows.
design_weaknesses: Some tasks are non-monotonic across batch size, so a mean-only caption would overstate the pattern.
No uncertainty or training-time/resource column is shown.
The page is dense even though only nine numeric columns are present.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: The visual story moves from Fig. 1’s raw-text batch → retriever similarity → in-batch attention → NTP/backprop pipeline, to Fig. 2’s exact architectural/mask insertion, then to Table 1 and Fig. 3’s retrieval comparisons. Fig. 4/5 test batch-size and LM-size factors. Appendix Fig. 6 gives a training-dynamics example, Fig. 7 gives a 16-chunk corpus batch, Tables 3–6 define benchmark/resources, Tables 7–10 expand per-task and matched controls, and Tables 11–19 cover scaling, mixed/OOD domains, and LM preservation.
cross_object_system.caption_system: Captions use a Figure/Table label followed by setup and metric/encoding definitions. Fig. 4/5 and Table 1 state headline findings; Fig. 3 states benchmark conclusions and appendix pointers. Table 2 is notably non-self-contained, only saying “Revela vs. Contriever Performance,” while glossary/resource captions prioritize identity over statistical definitions. No object reports uncertainty, error bars, intervals, or failure counts.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Result tables put Dataset/Task/Model at the left and model size or benchmark metrics in one or two header levels. Tables 1, 7, 8 use wide model-family headers; Tables 11–14 use nested three-way factor groups; Tables 15–19 use compact model-size columns. Booktabs-style top/mid/bottom rules and bold row winners are consistent; gray fill is reserved for supervised models in Table 1.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: The method vocabulary—Revela, retriever size, LM size, batch size, Wikipedia/code/Fineweb-edu corpus, CoIR/BRIGHT/BEIR, Contriever, and REPLUG—recurs across figures, tables, captions, and appendix sections. Main Table 1/Fig. 3 establish performance, Table 2 and Tables 9–10 isolate controls, Fig. 4/5 and Tables 11–18 expose scaling/domain factors, while Table 19 checks LM capacity preservation.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: Main objects are intentionally short: Table 1 and Fig. 3 use task means; Table 2 controls the backbone. Appendix A/B/C restore the omitted task rows, benchmark taxonomies, URLs/licenses, training example, Contriever setup, batch/LM-size interactions, mixed/OOD training, and LM results. The paper’s headline claims are readable in the main text but per-task heterogeneity and reproduction details depend on these appendix tables.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: PDF body/captions/tables use NimbusRomanNo9L and Computer Modern math with bold/italic variants; chart text uses DejaVu Sans-like sans-serif glyphs, and Figure 1 includes Georgia/Arial-like embedded labels. Table type is compact (approximately 6.5–8 pt body/header), while charts use small sans-serif ticks and direct labels. Colored hyperlink annotation boxes create additional non-semantic visual noise.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Blue/orange/green are reused for factor levels in Figures 4–5, while Figure 3 mixes family/opacity semantics and Figures 1/6/7 use local semantic colors. Bold is the dominant redundant cue in tables; Figure 1/6/7 add underline/italic, but Figures 3–5 rely mostly on hue/opacity. The palette is not uniformly grayscale safe and the PDF link overlays should be ignored when inferring semantic colors.

most_reusable_patterns: Draw the training signal as a concrete batch-to-retriever-to-attention-to-loss pipeline before introducing equations (Fig. 1 and Fig. 2).
Keep headline benchmark means in a paired bar figure, then publish per-task matrices with identical model/metric ordering in the appendix (Fig. 3 and Tables 7–8).
Represent scaling ablations with nested factor headers and matched CoIR/BEIR tables so batch size, retriever size, LM size, and domain composition remain separable (Fig. 4/5 and Tables 11–18).
Expose resource URLs/licenses and an illustrative batch/training snapshot as separate reproduction objects rather than mixing them into performance tables (Fig. 6/7 and Tables 3–6).
highest_value_objects: Fig. 1 (p.2) and Fig. 2 (p.4): the method interface and attention-mask insertion are the strongest mechanism visuals.
Table 1 (p.7) and Fig. 3 (p.7): the main retrieval comparison links CoIR, BRIGHT, BEIR, baseline family, and efficiency context.
Table 2 (p.8) plus Tables 9–10 (p.20): matched Contriever controls provide the clearest causal comparison within the otherwise broad leaderboard.
Tables 11–18 (pp.20–23): per-task scaling, mixed-domain, and OOD matrices prevent the broader generalization narrative from resting on means alone.
failure_patterns: The public repository has only rendered PNG counterparts; no editable plotting/table source exists for Figures 2/4–7 or Tables 2–19, and the BRIGHT/BEIR asset has revised values relative to the PDF.
Mean-only headline charts and bold-only tables provide no run variance, confidence interval, significance, failure count, or cost accounting despite efficiency/generalization claims.
Color and opacity are primary encodings in the bar figures; grayscale and small-screen readability are weak, while model labels are rotated or abbreviated.
Appendix tables are complete but dense, and many captions (especially Table 2) do not define metrics, aggregation, resource versions, or comparison conditions without surrounding prose.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: Translate raw-text co-training into a visible attention pipeline, use mean benchmark bars for the headline, and move every task-level, scaling, domain-shift, and reproduction detail into matched booktabs appendix matrices.
